title: The old man's horse
hook: a lost horse, a found herd, a broken leg, a son spared from war: who can say what is lucky? (Huainanzi 18)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zhuangzi grieved, and then drummed on a pot and sang. Your line was seasons turn. What sign of the season did you notice? Day fifty-five.

The job offer goes to someone else. Three months later, the company folds. The dream apartment comes through, and the upstairs neighbor turns out to play drums at midnight. Bad news that turns out good, good news that turns out hard: it's an old pattern, and it's easy to forget every time the next piece of news arrives. There's an old Chinese story about a man who doesn't forget. He lives near the frontier, where China meets the lands of the northern horse peoples. And one day, his horse runs away. Today's story is the old man's horse.
screen: `THE JOB GOES TO SOMEONE ELSE.` → `THEN THE COMPANY FOLDS.` → `THE OLD MAN'S HORSE RUNS AWAY.`

segments.voice: The horse gallops off across the border and is gone. The neighbors come to say how sorry they are. And the old man says: how do you know this isn't a blessing? Months later, the horse comes home, and it brings a herd of fine horses from the north with it. The neighbors come to congratulate him. And the old man says: how do you know this isn't a disaster? His son loves the new horses, and rides them, and one day falls and breaks his leg badly. He'll limp for life. The neighbors come to say how sorry they are. And the old man says: how do you know this isn't a blessing? A year later, raiders cross the border. Every able-bodied young man is called up to fight, and nine in ten of the men from the frontier die. The son, because of his leg, stays home. Father and son both live. That's the story, from a Chinese book called the Huainanzi, put together at a prince's court and drawing heavily on Taoist ideas. Today it lives on as a Chinese saying for when something goes wrong: the old man at the frontier lost his horse. Some modern retellings give the old man one word: maybe. Good luck? Maybe. Bad luck? Maybe. The old book puts it as a question, how do you know, but the heart is the same. We judge every event the instant it happens, as if the story were over. It never is. The old man isn't cold, and he isn't saying nothing matters. He just refuses to close the book on page one.
screen: `THE HORSE RUNS AWAY.` · `IT COMES BACK WITH A HERD.` · `THE SON BREAKS HIS LEG.` · `THE SON STAYS HOME FROM WAR.` · then, large: `HOW DO YOU KNOW?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet one bit of news with maybe. Breathe out first, slowly. Then find something from this week that got its label, good or bad, the moment it happened. Run the story forward, the way the neighbors never did: and then what? And then? Each time you reach a new turn, say maybe. Don't force it to be secretly good. Just leave the story open past page one. The bell holds the time.
Huainanzi. The old Chinese book that tells of a lost horse, a found herd, a broken leg, and a life spared, each time met with: how do you know?
Your line: maybe. Today, the next time something is instantly great or instantly terrible, say it inside: maybe. Then wait and see what comes back over the border. Day fifty-five.

howItsDone: In China the saying "the old man at the frontier lost his horse" is used to comfort someone after a setback, and the story is retold in Taoist and self-help settings, sometimes with the old man's answer shortened to "maybe".

original.note: Chinese, sài wēng shī mǎ: the old man at the frontier lost his horse, a four-word saying from this story.

what a scholar hears: Huainanzi chapter eighteen, a Han court compendium; the tale became the idiom sài wēng shī mǎ.

notes: Huainanzi 18 paraphrased; details: the horse flees to the Hu, returns with fine Hu horses, the son breaks his hip/thigh (髀), and nine in ten frontier men die when the Hu invade. The script says 'leg'; confirm.
Dating: presented to Emperor Wu around 139 BCE at the court of Liu An, prince of Huainan; described as 'drawing heavily on Taoist ideas' since the book is eclectic. Confirm framing.
The script says openly that 'maybe' is from modern retellings, since the carry uses it.
Chinese 塞翁失馬 (sài wēng shī mǎ): confirm; the full saying continues 焉知非福.
Index calls the book 'Huainanzi 18'; the outline sits this in the Taoist week.
